newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan turns to World Bank for finance chief.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan turns to World Bank for finance chief.

text.p: Pakistan's caretaker government will turn over charge of the ailing economy to a World Bank executive who was a stern critic of ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto's policies, officials said on Thursday.
World Bank vice-president Javed Burki, a Pakistani national, will be adviser to the Finance Ministry but in charge of finance, economic affairs and planning, a senior government official said.
"He (Burki) is going to join the government," the official said. "He will be adviser for finance, economic affairs and planning, and be effectively in charge of these divisions of the government."

Under World Bank rules, Burki, who would take temporary leave from his post at the Washington-based development bank, could not accept the finance minister position, said the official, who asked not to be identified.
The official said there was no need for a finance minister in the interim government, which took office on Tuesday after Bhutto's government was abruptly dismissed.

President Farooq Leghari, who sacked Bhutto, set general elections for February 3, 1997. That would give Burki less than three months to try to turn around the economy, saddled by burdensome debt, a burgeoning trade deficit and high inflation.

It was not the first time Pakistan has looked to the World Bank's ranks for expertise. In 1993, Moeen Qureshi, like Burki a Pakistani national and World Bank executive, served as interim prime minister, swiftly putting together a controversial loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund.
Critics of Qureshi say the loan was tied to an austerity plan which proved too ambitious and stirred resentment.
Burki sharply criticised Pakistan's economic management in a recent series of interviews and articles in which he analysed what he called a dozen "faultlines" in Pakistan's economy.
Burki listed 12 problems plaguing Pakistan's economy, including a serious budget deficit, growing debt and rapid population growth.

While Burki did not mention Bhutto by name, she appeared irritated by the articles, with newspapers quoting her in mid-September as denouncing "some World Bank officials in Washington" for creating problems for her government.
Burki, who was expected to arrive in Islamabad by Friday, would take charge at a crucial juncture.
On Wednesday, Moody's Investors Service lowered Pakistan's sovereign ceiling foreign-currency debt rating to B2 from B1.

The New York-based credit rating agency said the downgrade reflected "the increased fragility of Pakistan's liquidity position and the severe pressures that the large domestic and foreign-currency debt burden exert on public finances, the external accounts and official reserves".
Pakistan is negotiating an agreement with the International Monetary Fund over a stalled $600 million standby loan considered crucial for shoring up the nation's finances.
Talks between an IMF team and Pakistan continued this week despite the abrupt change of government, but the deal is taking longer than earlier expected.
Sartaj Aziz, finance minister in a former government led by Nawaz Sharif, told Reuters that Burki was expected to focus on taming corruption and mismanagement in the administration.
"Now we will see a revival of the economic decline," Aziz said. "The economy should start moving forward."
